evaluated.name: Financing Gap Meets Illiquidity
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose capital spending exceeds operating cash flow must raise external funds; when it simultaneously holds little cash against near-term liabilities, the investment program is a genuine solvency risk rather than a growth option, and expected returns embed value destruction and dilution risk.
evaluated.reasoning: The capex-minus-operating-cash-flow gap measures external finance dependence directly, and the cash-to-current-liabilities term measures the buffer available to survive the funding period. Only the intersection — large gap plus thin liquidity — identifies fragile expansion, while a large gap at a cash-rich firm is ordinary growth investment. The interaction therefore isolates urgent balance-sheet strain rather than the isolated investment or liquidity effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Buildup Under Working Capital Strain
evaluated.hypothesis: Rising inventories are benign when a firm has ample working capital but signal unsold product, forced production, and imminent liquidity trouble when net working capital is already negative, so the joint occurrence predicts subsequent write-downs and poor returns.
evaluated.reasoning: Inventory investment is the most reversible and most demand-sensitive component of firm investment, so it is the cleanest place to detect involuntary expansion. Conditioning on negative working capital separates a demand-driven stock build (financed comfortably) from a distress-driven one (financed by stretching payables). The interaction targets a mechanism distinct from fixed-capital or total-asset growth signals.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Surge Against Cash-Flow Debt Service
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm spending far above its own recent capital-budget norm is only penalized when its operating cash flow is too thin to service existing liabilities; that combination signals an escalation that must be funded externally under stress, whereas a distressed firm spending below its own norm is credibly retrenching to preserve solvency.
evaluated.reasoning: The investment leg is a firm-relative capex surge (capex versus its own three-year average), not total asset growth, so it is orthogonal to the Cooper-Gulen-Schill construct and to CMA; the distress leg is the Beaver/Ohlson cash-flow-to-liabilities ratio rather than a leverage tilt. Centering the investment term with ZSCORE and weighting it by a distress rank in [0,1] makes the signal near-zero for financially sound firms, so the spread is a genuine interaction with an interpretable long leg (distressed retrenchers) rather than an amplified investment main effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Industry-Relative Capex Under Accumulated Deficit
evaluated.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, at)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(wcap, at)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Capital spending above industry norm is value-destroying specifically for firms carrying an accumulated earnings deficit and thin net working capital, because these firms lack the internal funds and liquidity slack to complete the program, while the same distressed firms spending below industry norm are conserving cash and are undervalued.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the binary retained-earnings dummy with a continuous, ranked two-component distress score (the retained-earnings and working-capital terms of the Altman construct) removes the mass of tied zeros, so both legs of the sort contain live firms and the signal varies within the distressed population as the hypothesis requires. Industry z-scoring the capex intensity strips out capital-intensity differences, ensuring the interaction reflects firm-specific aggressiveness rather than sector membership.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered Retrenchment Toward Liquidity
evaluated.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, at), 1)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Among highly levered firms, a deliberate rotation of the balance sheet out of fixed assets and into cash is a solvency-restoring action that the market underweights; the same rotation at an unlevered firm carries no information because there is no solvency constraint to relieve.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the additive asset-growth-plus-profitability composite (which FF5's CMA and RMW legs largely span) with a change-in-asset-composition variable that no standard factor prices: it is the shift in cash intensity minus the shift in fixed-capital intensity. Multiplying by the leverage rank makes the effect exist only where the mechanism operates, so the long leg is levered firms converting hard assets into liquidity and the short leg is levered firms sinking cash into fixed capital.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Financed at Short Maturity
evaluated.hypothesis: Long-lived capital investment funded against a heavy stock of debt maturing within a year creates a maturity mismatch: the asset pays off over a decade while the liability must be rolled next quarter, so these firms bear rollover risk that is punished when credit conditions tighten.
evaluated.reasoning: This is a distinct fragility channel from leverage level or liquidity buffer — a firm can be modestly levered and still be dangerously short-funded — and it interacts naturally with the duration of the investment being made. The distress leg scales current debt by current assets, the pool actually available to retire it, so the signal isolates mismatch rather than size or leverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Headcount Expansion Without Debt Service Capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: Adding employees is a quasi-fixed commitment that is far harder to reverse than capex; when a firm expands headcount while earnings are too small relative to its liability stock, it is locking in an operating cost base it cannot fund, and subsequent layoffs and restructuring charges are underpriced.
evaluated.reasoning: This moves the investment leg off the balance sheet entirely and onto the real side, so it cannot be a rescaling of asset growth, capex intensity, or any accrual-based construct already in the archive. Because labor commitments carry no collateral value, the distress interaction should be sharper for employment growth than for capital growth — a directly testable contrast against the capex-based signals in this batch.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered Firms Sweating Installed Capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: Among highly levered firms, rising sales per unit of installed property and equipment shows management generating growth from assets already owned rather than from new commitments; this capital-efficient resilience is undervalued, while levered firms whose capacity utilization is falling are heading toward covenant trouble.
evaluated.reasoning: The gen-0 positive-sign attempt failed (alpha -1.7% against a positive prediction) because balance-sheet rotation into cash is itself a distress symptom rather than a discipline signal; utilization improvement is a genuine operating-performance channel that separates resilient levered firms from shrinking ones. Centering the utilization change and weighting by the leverage rank means unlevered firms contribute near zero, so both legs are populated by levered firms and the spread is an interaction rather than a leverage tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Stop-Start Capital Budgeting Under Deficit
evaluated.hypothesis: Erratic, stop-start capital spending reveals that a firm's investment is dictated by whatever financing happens to be available rather than by a stable opportunity set; when this instability coincides with an accumulated earnings deficit relative to the liability stock, projects get started and abandoned, sunk costs are written off, and returns disappoint.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the level-of-investment channel entirely for a second-moment channel — the volatility of the investment rate over three years — which is not a rescaling of capex intensity, asset growth, or any archived signal. The distress leg uses the accumulated deficit scaled by liabilities, a stock measure of never-having-earned that is conceptually independent of the flow coverage ratios used elsewhere in the archive, and the long leg is the economically meaningful case of fragile firms with steady, planned capital budgets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Soft-Asset Expansion Without Earnings Cushion
evaluated.hypothesis: Expansion that adds intangible and goodwill-type assets rather than tangible capacity produces collateral that lenders will not accept and that must be impaired if performance disappoints; when the acquiring firm's pretax income is small relative to its liabilities, such soft-asset growth signals overpayment and imminent write-downs rather than franchise building.
evaluated.reasoning: The asset-quality composition of investment is a channel untouched by the archive, which has so far tested capex, inventory, headcount, and total-asset growth — all of which are collateralizable in a way intangibles are not, so the distress interaction should be sharply stronger here. Pretax income scaled by liabilities captures the debt-service cushion that determines whether an impairment triggers covenant trouble, giving a clean conditional reading rather than a repackaged profitability tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Escalating Capex Into Deteriorating Profitability
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not a level: a firm whose return on assets has been sliding for several years and which nevertheless raises capital spending is escalating commitment to a failing business, while a firm on the same downward trajectory that cuts spending is adapting, and the market prices the two alike.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing a static distress ratio with the multi-year slope of profitability makes the conditioning variable a state transition rather than an Altman-style level, so the signal cannot load on the RMW-like main effect that static profitability proxies carry. Centering the capex-growth leg while keeping the deterioration weight in [0,1] means healthy or improving firms contribute near zero, so both extremes of the sort are populated by deteriorating firms and the spread isolates the escalation-versus-adaptation contrast.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Fire-Sale Disinvestment Under Weak Coverage
evaluated.hypothesis: For firms whose earnings cannot cover their liability stock, shrinking the productive asset base is not disciplined retrenchment but forced liquidation at depressed prices, which destroys future earning capacity and predicts continued underperformance.
evaluated.reasoning: Every archived signal assumes the investment-distress relation is monotone decreasing, yet if distressed disinvestment is also punished the relation is U-shaped and the true mechanism is asset-base instability rather than overinvestment — a possibility no prior test can distinguish. This is the cheapest available test of that structural question, and it directly informs whether future long legs should be built from distressed retrenchers at all.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Growth Financed by Deteriorating Current Position
evaluated.hypothesis: Stock building is most dangerous when it is being financed by stretching payables and other current obligations, so that the current position is visibly deteriorating in the same year the inventory is added; the firm is converting near-term liquidity into unsold goods.
evaluated.reasoning: The archive's best-alpha inventory signal conditioned on the *level* of working capital, which the critic correctly noted is mechanically linked to inventory itself; conditioning instead on the *year-over-year deterioration in the current ratio* breaks that mechanical overlap and identifies the financing source of the buildup rather than its accounting footprint. This isolates static-versus-dynamic distress conditioning within the family that has worked best.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained Investment While Deleveraging
evaluated.hypothesis: Investment carries opposite information depending on the direction of balance-sheet repair: a firm that maintains a high investment rate while simultaneously reducing its liability ratio is funding growth internally and demonstrating genuine operating strength, whereas the same investment rate alongside rising liabilities is externally financed expansion.
evaluated.reasoning: Both prior positive-sign attempts failed because they defined resilience as *low* investment, which loads on CMA and is indistinguishable from the published asset-growth effect; this defines resilience as high investment financed without new liabilities, which is the economically correct reading of self-funded capacity and is orthogonal to the conservative-investment factor. It is the direct mirror of the batch's negative signals and gives the long leg an interpretable, populated definition.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Building Into Shrinking Revenue
evaluated.hypothesis: Distress often arrives through the top line first: a firm whose revenue is contracting while it continues to add productive capacity is building assets for demand that has already disappeared, producing idle capacity, impairments, and eventual forced retrenchment.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the cash-slack conditioning the critic identified as double-counted with a demand-side fragility measure — revenue contraction — that appears nowhere in the archive and is conceptually independent of leverage, liquidity, and the cash balance. It also sharpens the mechanism: the destructive case is capacity added against falling demand, and the long leg is firms investing into genuine revenue growth, both of which are populated and interpretable.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Accumulated Capital Vintage Against Thin Equity Cushion
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a fragile firm is not this year's spending but the stock of recent commitments embedded in its asset base; a firm whose gross plant is mostly the product of the last five years' spending has an unproven, unamortized capital vintage, and if its book equity is thin relative to liabilities, any shortfall in the returns from that vintage is absorbed by creditors rather than cushioned.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the one-year escalation framing entirely for a stock-of-commitments channel — five-year cumulative capex as a share of gross plant measures how young and untested the installed base is, which no archived signal captures. The equity-to-liabilities cushion is a solvency variable (ceq is new to the archive) rather than a flow profitability measure, so the interaction cannot collapse into the q-theory investment-profitability effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Aging Capital Stock Under Current Liability Pressure
evaluated.hypothesis: A low ratio of net to gross plant means the asset base is heavily depreciated and has not been renewed; when the firm simultaneously faces current liabilities in excess of current assets, the deferred maintenance is a symptom of an inability to fund replacement capital, and competitive decline follows.
evaluated.reasoning: The tax framing is dropped because txt is effectively a profitability transform; this substitutes an asset-age channel measured purely from the plant accounts, which is a level concept absent from the archive and orthogonal to earnings. Paired with the accepted fire-sale disinvestment test, it lets the generation distinguish whether distressed *under*-investment is punished through forced sales, through deferred renewal, or not at all.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Acquisitions On A Thin Equity Base
evaluated.hypothesis: Acquisition spending is the least reversible and most agency-prone form of investment; undertaken by a firm whose book equity is thin relative to its asset base, it is effectively a levered bet where creditors bear the downside, and integration failure translates directly into solvency stress.
evaluated.reasoning: The acquisition channel is completely untested in the archive even though it is where the "value-destroying expansion" story is most literal, and treating an unreported aqc as zero acquisition activity is the economically correct convention rather than a coverage patch. Book-equity thinness is a solvency measure rather than a flow or liquidity measure, so the pairing does not replicate any existing distress leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Multi-Year Capacity Retreat Under Leverage
evaluated.hypothesis: A single year of shrinking plant is often ordinary depreciation or a disposal, but a productive asset base sitting at the bottom of its own five-year range signals a firm that has been retreating from its industry for years; when carried alongside heavy liabilities, that retreat is a solvency-driven withdrawal rather than a strategic focus.
evaluated.reasoning: The fire-sale test produced the archive's most reliable alpha but a wrong-signed slope because one-year plant growth is contaminated by the monotone asset-growth effect; replacing the change with a position-in-own-history state measures the persistence of retreat and should be far less collinear with that known force. If the slope and the alpha align here, it confirms that the disinvestment mechanism is real and that the earlier contradiction was a specification issue rather than an economic one.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capex Amid Lengthening Operating Cycle
evaluated.hypothesis: When non-cash current assets rise relative to sales, the firm is taking longer to convert production into cash — receivables are aging and goods are sitting — and a firm that adds fixed capacity while its operating cycle is stretching is committing long-term funds precisely as its short-term cash conversion deteriorates.
evaluated.reasoning: This drops the maturity-mismatch rescaling for a cash-conversion channel: the conditioner is the year-over-year change in working-capital intensity of revenue, which measures operating deterioration rather than the cash-holdings or short-debt dimensions already spanned by the archive. All four inputs are high-coverage balance-sheet and income items, so it should retain roughly 0.12 coverage while testing a fragility concept — operating-cycle stretch — that no archived signal contains.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Growth While Claims Outrun Revenue
evaluated.hypothesis: Solvency is a race between the growth of obligations and the growth of the revenue that must service them; a firm expanding gross plant while its liabilities compound faster than its sales is building capacity on a claim structure the business is not growing into.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the MIN experiment with a growth-rate mismatch makes the distress leg a dynamic solvency concept — the wedge between liability growth and revenue growth — rather than another level ratio drawn from the same balance-sheet dimensions already tested. It also avoids the correlation problem the critic identified, since the conditioner is a difference of growth rates and is close to orthogonal to the level of leverage, liquidity, or profitability.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Investing Through Chronic Losses
evaluated.hypothesis: One loss year is a shock; three or four losses in five years is a business model that does not work, and a firm that keeps its investment rate high across a sustained run of losses is funding a franchise the market has already learned cannot earn its cost of capital.
evaluated.reasoning: The extraordinary-items construct was accounting-incorrect, so the write-off idea is replaced by loss persistence — the count of loss years over five years, the Ohlson-style state variable — which the expression computes exactly and which no archived distress leg uses. Persistence is distinct from the *level* of profitability because a firm with a single deep loss year scores low here while a chronically marginal firm scores high, so the signal cannot collapse into the q-theory investment-profitability interaction.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Post-Investment Cash Surplus Among Levered Firms
evaluated.hypothesis: For a levered firm the decisive quantity is cash left after the capital program has been paid for, because that surplus is what retires debt; levered firms generating a post-investment surplus are deleveraging under their own power and are priced as if their leverage were a permanent risk, while levered firms with a post-investment deficit must return to markets.
evaluated.reasoning: The inverted ib/capx ratio is replaced by the correctly oriented free-cash-flow-after-investment measure, which is numerically stable, keeps capex in the numerator with the right sign, and is the exact quantity that determines debt-service capacity rather than a low-investment tilt. The leverage rank places unlevered firms near the middle of the sort, so both legs are populated by levered firms and the spread contrasts self-funding levered firms against externally dependent ones.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Forced Conservatism On A Thin Equity Cushion
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm whose gross plant is contracting and whose remaining plant is heavily depreciated is not practising capital discipline — it is unable to fund renewal; when its book equity is also thin relative to liabilities, the apparent conservatism is a solvency constraint, and the conservative-investment premium the market prices into such firms fails to materialise.
evaluated.reasoning: The three archived signals with the most reliable negative alphas each captured one facet of this state (plant contraction, asset age, multi-year retreat) separately; combining contraction and age into a single ranked disinvestment score should identify forced conservatism far more precisely than either leg alone while keeping both legs high-coverage. The equity cushion conditions on whether the retreat is voluntary, which is exactly the distinction the FF5 benchmark cannot make.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Contraction Against A Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: When a large share of a firm's debt comes due within the year, shrinking the productive asset base is the signature of assets being sold to meet maturities; the firm is liquidating earning capacity to pay claims, which permanently lowers future cash flows.
evaluated.reasoning: Maturity structure is the one distress dimension in the archive whose signal produced a correctly signed cross-sectional slope (Capex Financed at Short Maturity, fmb -2.20), while capacity contraction is the leg driving the largest alphas — pairing them targets both forms of evidence rather than one. Using the short-debt *share* of total liabilities rather than a scaled level isolates refinancing urgency from leverage magnitude, so the signal is not a repackaged leverage tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Sustained Acquisitiveness With No Equity Buffer
evaluated.hypothesis: A single acquisition is an event, but five years of cumulative acquisition spending is a strategy of buying rather than building growth; carried out from a thin equity base, that strategy leaves a firm with unproven acquired assets, integration liabilities, and no cushion when the acquired earnings disappoint.
evaluated.reasoning: The one-year acquisition signal delivered a -3.3% alpha but the critic correctly noted that a large tied mass at zero collapses most of the cross-section onto pure book leverage; cumulating five years of spending sharply reduces the zero bucket and shifts the construct from an event to a strategy, which is what the hypothesis actually claims. It consolidates a demonstrated winner while removing the diagnostic weakness that made its interaction claim ambiguous.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Scale Instability Without Debt Service Capacity
evaluated.hypothesis: The archive shows that fragile firms are punished both when they expand and when they contract, which means the operative variable is not the direction of adjustment but its magnitude: a firm with insufficient earnings to cover its liabilities that is violently resizing its labor force and capital base in either direction is adjusting under duress, while a fragile firm holding scale steady is managing its constraints.
evaluated.reasoning: This resolves rather than repeats the sign contradiction the critic identified — Headcount Expansion (fmb -2.54) and Fire-Sale Disinvestment (alpha -3.5%) used the same NEG(ib/lt) conditioner with opposite investment signs and both worked, which is only coherent if the relation is U-shaped in adjustment magnitude. Taking absolute growth in both factor inputs and ranking their sum tests that U-shape directly, a hypothesis no archived signal can express.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Borrowing Beyond Investment Needs
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(SUB(DELTA(ADD(dltt, dlc), 1), capx), at)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(ib, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: New debt raised in excess of the year's capital spending is not funding growth — it is funding liquidity, working capital losses, or the repayment of other claims; when the borrower's earnings already fail to cover its liability stock, such defensive borrowing is a pre-distress drawdown rather than an expansion decision.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the sign-fitted cash-rotation re-test with a forward-stated hypothesis about the *purpose* of financing: the wedge between debt issuance and capital expenditure identifies borrowing that has no investment counterpart, a construct absent from the archive and distinct from leverage level, leverage change, and net issuance. The interaction is essential rather than decorative, because the same excess borrowing at a firm with ample earnings coverage is ordinary balance-sheet management.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Levered Firms Whose Asset Base Outgrows Their Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: For a levered firm the resilience case is one where productive capacity is growing faster than the claims against it, so that each unit of debt is supported by more earning assets every year; the opposite case — claims compounding faster than the asset base that services them — is a slow slide toward insolvency.
evaluated.reasoning: Turnover-based resilience is dropped for a balance-sheet race between capacity growth and liability growth, which is a different economic quantity from asset productivity and is measured on the stock rather than the flow side. Winsorizing the growth difference addresses the small-denominator tail problem the critic raised, and the leverage rank keeps both legs populated by levered firms so the spread is not a leverage tilt.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Buildup Against A Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: Converting cash into unsold goods is most dangerous when a large share of the firm's debt matures within the year: the working capital is locked in exactly when the claims come due, forcing either a distressed inventory liquidation or a refinancing on unfavourable terms.
evaluated.reasoning: This crosses the archive's two most productive legs from opposite families — inventory growth carries a correctly signed slope and a -3.1% alpha with a raw Sharpe of -0.35, while the short-maturity share produced the strongest alpha t-statistic in the archive (-4.72) — so the pairing is the most direct route to joint slope-and-alpha evidence rather than one or the other. Neither leg is a rescaling of the other and both are high-coverage annual balance-sheet items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Unpledgeable Assets Against Near-Term Maturities
evaluated.hypothesis: Refinancing capacity depends on what can be pledged; a firm whose asset base is predominantly intangible has little secured borrowing capacity, so when a large fraction of its debt comes due it must refinance unsecured or sell operating assets, and the market underprices that collateral constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: Collateral quality is a genuinely new dimension of the interaction — every archived signal treats investment as a flow and distress as leverage, liquidity, or earnings, whereas this treats the *composition* of accumulated investment as the determinant of financing capacity. It also gives the maturity-wall mechanism a second, independent test with an investment leg that is a stock rather than a growth rate, so a confirming result cannot be attributed to the asset-growth effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Terming Out Debt While Still Investing
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm that lengthens its debt maturity profile while maintaining its capital program has convinced creditors to fund it on long terms — the clearest market-validated evidence of resilience — whereas a firm whose maturity profile is shortening while it keeps spending is being financed only at the front end.
evaluated.reasoning: Four positive-sign attempts have failed because they defined resilience through low investment, cash rotation, or turnover; this defines it through the *maturity structure creditors are willing to grant*, which is an external validation rather than a management choice and is untested in the archive. It is the natural long-side complement to the maturity-wall mechanism that has produced the archive's most reliable alpha.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Goodwill-Inflated Cushion Behind The Claims
evaluated.hypothesis: What protects creditors is tangible book equity, not accounting equity: a firm whose balance sheet carries large goodwill from past acquisitions while its equity net of that goodwill is thin relative to liabilities has a cushion that will evaporate at the first impairment, so the recorded solvency overstates the true solvency.
evaluated.reasoning: This is not another asset-growth-times-constraint cell; the investment leg is the *stock* of capitalized past acquisition premia and the distress leg is the quality rather than the size of the equity cushion, a construct that no archived signal contains. Treating an unreported goodwill balance as zero is the economically correct convention, and the interaction is essential because goodwill intensity is harmless when tangible equity is ample and lethal when it is not.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Far Below Its Own Peak At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: A firm operating with gross plant far below the peak it reached in the last five years has permanently given up capacity rather than paused expansion; when a large share of its debt matures within the year, that drawdown from peak reflects assets already sold or written off to service claims.
evaluated.reasoning: Industry demeaning was cosmetic; replacing the one-year growth rate with a drawdown-from-own-peak level is the substantive respecification the slope/alpha conflict calls for, because the published asset-growth effect operates on annual growth rates while a five-year peak distance measures a persistent state and should be far less collinear with it. If the Fama-MacBeth slope turns negative while the maturity-wall alpha survives, the contraction mechanism is validated on both forms of evidence for the first time.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Equity Raised Beyond Investment Needs
evaluated.hypothesis: Equity sold in excess of the year's capital spending is not funding projects — it is funding the retirement of claims or the replacement of lost working capital; when the firm simultaneously faces a large share of debt maturing within the year, the issuance is a creditor-driven rescue rather than an owner-driven investment decision.
evaluated.reasoning: Netting capital expenditure out of the issuance measure directly addresses the critique that raw sstk/at is the published share-issuance anomaly: a growth firm raising equity to fund a large capital program now scores near zero, while a firm raising equity it does not invest scores high, which is precisely the rescue-financing construct the hypothesis describes. The maturity-wall conditioner then separates rescue issuance from opportunistic issuance, making the interaction the identifying element rather than a tilt on a known main effect.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Overhang State At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: What matters for a firm facing near-term maturities is not how fast inventory grew last year but whether the stock of goods is unusually large relative to the revenue it must generate; a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year inventory-to-sales range has an overhang that will only clear through discounting.
evaluated.reasoning: This isolates a specific design choice on the archive's best joint signal — a persistent state versus a one-year flow — which matters because the flow version may work only through the accrual and asset-growth components it shares with published effects, whereas the state version is scaled by revenue and cannot be. If the state version retains the alpha and the slope, the mechanism is genuinely about stock overhang meeting rollover risk rather than about growth accounting.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquidity Lock-Up Against Composite Fragility
evaluated.hypothesis: Rollover risk and a thin equity cushion are distinct fragilities that compound: a firm with debt maturing soon can survive if owners have capital at risk behind it, and a thinly capitalized firm can survive if nothing is due, but the firm exposed to both cannot absorb an inventory write-down.
evaluated.reasoning: The two conditioners that produced the archive's strongest alphas — the short-maturity share and the equity cushion — have never been combined, and because one measures the timing of claims while the other measures the capital behind them they should be complementary rather than redundant. Ranking their sum keeps the conditioner bounded and well-populated, preserving the aligned slope-and-alpha property of the inventory-growth investment leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Long And Lengthening Maturity With Sustained Investment
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), DELTA(RATIO(dlc, lt), 1)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Creditors reveal what they believe: a firm that is investing while its debt is both long-dated and getting longer has been granted funding on patient terms, and that endorsement is the resilience the market underprices; a firm investing while its maturity profile shortens is being financed only at the front end.
evaluated.reasoning: Terming Out Debt While Still Investing was the first positive-sign signal in this archive to deliver a real alpha (+2.9%, t=+2.70), and its weakness is that a one-year change in maturity mix is noisy and can reflect a single refinancing; requiring the *level* to be long as well as the change to be lengthening identifies firms with durably patient capital. This is a substantive strengthening of the conditioner rather than a re-scaling of the investment leg.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Capacity Growth With Falling Labor Productivity
evaluated.hypothesis: Revenue per employee is the cleanest read on whether a firm's existing operations are working; adding plant while output per worker is deteriorating means the firm is scaling a process that is already losing efficiency, and the new capacity will dilute returns further.
evaluated.reasoning: Every distress leg in this archive is financial — leverage, maturity, liquidity, earnings, equity cushion — whereas operating efficiency measured on the labor base is an economic fragility that precedes the financial symptoms and is untested here. It also gives the generation one genuinely different axis, so a null result would tell us the interaction requires a balance-sheet constraint rather than merely deteriorating operations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Receivables Lock-Up At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: If the mechanism behind the archive's best joint signal is genuinely about liquidity being locked into unconvertible assets, it should operate through receivables as well as goods: a firm that has extended far more credit to customers while a large share of its own debt matures within the year has financed its buyers instead of its lenders.
evaluated.reasoning: Subtracting inventory as well as cash removes the double-count the critic identified and leaves a receivables-and-other-current-asset channel that is genuinely disjoint from the parent signal's leg, making this a discrimination test rather than a re-pairing. If it works, the mechanism is general working-capital lock-up meeting rollover risk; if only the inventory version works, the effect is about unsold product specifically, and either answer directs the final generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Operating Intangibles Against Near-Term Maturities
evaluated.hypothesis: Intangible assets excluding acquisition goodwill — capitalized software, patents, licences — are the assets a lender will not take as security and a buyer will not pay for in a hurry; a firm whose balance sheet is built on them and whose debt matures within the year has no collateral to post when the refinancing conversation begins.
evaluated.reasoning: Pooling plant with intangibles would have confounded pledgeability further, so instead this strips goodwill out of the intangible measure, which directly tests the critic's concern that the -4.9% alpha of the parent signal may be inherited from acquisition legacy rather than from collateral quality. Treating an unreported goodwill balance as zero is the correct accounting convention here, and the residual non-goodwill intangible intensity is the cleanest available proxy for unpledgeable operating assets.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual Lock-Up Overhang At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Liquidity can be locked up in goods or in customer credit, and a firm sitting at the top of its own five-year range on both — with a large share of debt maturing within the year — has committed its entire operating liquidity to assets it cannot convert before the claims fall due.
evaluated.reasoning: The two channels have now been tested separately against the same conditioner and both produced slopes near -3.5 with negative alphas, and because receivables are measured here net of inventory the two ranked states are genuinely disjoint rather than double-counted. Scaling each by sales and ranking within firm history preserves the state construction that beat the growth-rate version, so this should compound the two effects rather than dilute either.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Overhang Against Pure Maturity Structure
evaluated.hypothesis: What creates rollover pressure is the share of *borrowing* that must be repaid within the year, not the share of total liabilities: a firm whose debt is overwhelmingly short-dated faces a refinancing decision every twelve months, and if its inventory is simultaneously at an historic high relative to sales it will meet that decision without liquid resources.
evaluated.reasoning: The conditioner behind every large alpha in this archive is dlc/lt, whose denominator includes payables, accruals and deferred items, so the critic's standing concern that it partly proxies for total leverage has never been tested; replacing the denominator with total interest-bearing debt isolates maturity structure from leverage magnitude. If the alpha and slope survive, the mechanism is confirmed as refinancing timing rather than a leverage tilt, which is the single most valuable robustness result available before the final generations.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Overhang Against Cash Coverage Of Maturities
evaluated.hypothesis: Rollover risk only binds when the firm cannot simply pay: a maturity wall is harmless for a firm holding cash in excess of what is due, so the fragility that interacts with inventory overhang is the shortfall of cash against near-term debt, not the size of that debt.
evaluated.reasoning: This reformulates the conditioner as a coverage ratio rather than a share, which places every cash-rich firm at the benign end regardless of its debt structure — an economically sharper definition of the constraint than dlc/lt, and one that directly tests whether the mechanism runs through payment capacity. Together with S2 it decomposes the archive's workhorse conditioner into its two candidate economic contents, timing and coverage.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Duration Extension And Earnings Cover For An Investing Firm
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(RATIO(capx, ppent)), RANK(SUMRANK(NEG(DELTA(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, dltt)), 1)), RATIO(ib, lt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: An investing firm is resilient when two conditions hold together: its debt mix is shifting toward long maturities, and its earnings actually cover the liability stock; that combination means the capital program is being funded patiently by creditors who can see the cash flow servicing it.
evaluated.reasoning: The critique is well taken that long-term debt *growth* puts the long leg inside the external-financing anomaly and explodes off a small base, so the conditioner is rebuilt from a bounded maturity-mix change — the share of interest-bearing debt that is short-dated, differenced — which contains no issuance quantity at all. Adding earnings coverage to that mix change ensures the long leg is investing firms that can pay rather than firms merely holding little short-term debt, which was the collapse mode of the archived version.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Liquid Reserve Shifting Into Goods At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: Within a firm's convertible resources, the split between cash and unsold goods determines whether a maturity can be met; a firm whose cash share of that pool has fallen sharply has rotated repayment capacity into product just as its debt comes due.
evaluated.reasoning: Expressing the rotation as the change in a bounded share — cash divided by cash plus inventory, which lies in the unit interval — removes the unbounded cash-growth term the critic identified as noise-dominating while measuring exactly the same reallocation decision. Because it is a composition change rather than a level or a growth rate, it is also cleanly distinct from both the archived inventory-growth and inventory-overhang legs.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Nothing Convertible Behind The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: When debt falls due the only assets that matter are those convertible within weeks — cash and receivables; a firm whose balance sheet holds few quick assets relative to its size, whatever the reason, must refinance or sell operating assets at a discount, and the market underprices that constraint.
evaluated.reasoning: Fusing inventory overhang with intangible intensity would have combined two legs that are negatively correlated across industries, so instead this replaces them with the single balance-sheet-wide quantity both were proxying: the share of assets that are genuinely quick, current assets net of inventory. It subsumes the intangible-heavy and inventory-heavy cases in one coherent measure, keeps the conditioner that produced every large alpha in the archive, and uses only high-coverage annual items.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Inventory Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage
evaluated.hypothesis: Rollover pressure is properly measured as debt due divided by the assets that can actually pay it — cash and receivables — rather than as a share of total liabilities; a firm whose maturing debt exceeds its quick assets and whose inventory is at an historic high has no route to repayment other than refinancing.
evaluated.reasoning: Two conditioner reformulations were tested last generation and both were informative but weaker than dlc/lt, which suggests the missing ingredient is not maturity structure or cash alone but the ratio of what is due to what is convertible; this construction embeds the quick-asset insight that produced the archive's largest alpha directly into the conditioner. It also avoids the near-zero denominator instability of che/dlc, since quick assets are strictly positive for essentially all firms.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Dual Overhang Against Quick-Asset Coverage
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUMRANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5), TS_RANK(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, SUB(act, invt))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The firms that underperform are those whose operating liquidity is simultaneously consumed on both working-capital channels and whose maturing debt is large relative to the quick assets left over; both conditions are needed, and each is measured on the dimension that matters.
evaluated.reasoning: This pairs the investment leg with the archive's strongest cross-sectional slope against the coverage-based conditioner motivated in S2, so it is the leanest combination of the two best-validated components rather than a stack of everything. Running it alongside S1 and S2 also decomposes cleanly: if S5 beats both parents, the improvement comes from the conditioner; if S1 beats S5, it comes from adding the structural quick-asset level.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Releasing Working Capital While Terming Out Debt
evaluated.hypothesis: The resilience case is a firm actively converting its balance sheet back into cash and using that flexibility to push its debt out: destocking relative to sales frees liquidity, and a falling short-debt share shows creditors accepting longer terms, together describing a firm repairing itself before it is forced to.
evaluated.reasoning: The one long-side mechanism that has produced alpha in this archive is creditor-granted maturity extension (+3.6%, t=+3.04), and pairing it with working-capital release rather than with capital spending removes the investment-anomaly headwind that the critic identified as the weakness of the capex-based version. It is the precise economic mirror of the flagship short signal, so a positive result would confirm the interaction is continuous across the whole distribution rather than a tail phenomenon.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Consumed And Structural Illiquidity Conjunction
evaluated.expression: MUL(MIN(RANK(TS_RANK(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), RANK(NEG(RATIO(SUB(act, invt), at)))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The defenceless firm is one where liquidity has recently been consumed *and* there was structurally little of it to begin with; a firm with a fat quick-asset base can absorb an inventory overhang, and a structurally illiquid firm with lean, well-managed stock can still meet its maturities from receipts.
evaluated.reasoning: Replacing the nested SUMRANK with a minimum removes the silent double-weighting the critic identified and makes the construction a faithful conjunction: the composite is high only when the weaker of the two illiquidity readings is also extreme, so attribution is unambiguous. Because the recent-state leg carries the archive's strongest slope and the structural-level leg its strongest alpha, the conjunction is the cleanest available test of whether they are complements rather than a weighted average of parents.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Weeks-Of-Sales Overhang Weighted By Rollover Risk
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: The damage from an inventory overhang scales with its size in weeks of sales, not with where it ranks in the cross-section, and that magnitude should be amplified in proportion to how much debt is coming due — a firm two months of sales above its norm facing a maturity wall is in a materially different position from one a day above it.
evaluated.reasoning: The previous version collapsed the cardinal deviation back to an ordering with an outer RANK, so this leaves the deviation in its natural units — winsorized at the one-percent tails for robustness — and lets the magnitude enter the product directly against the bounded conditioner rank. That makes the signal genuinely magnitude-weighted rather than rank-weighted, which is the design question the flagship mechanism still has open.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Customer Credit Outrunning Revenue At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.expression: MUL(RANK(SUB(GROWTH(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), 1), GROWTH(sale, 1))), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: When receivables grow faster than the revenue they supposedly represent, the firm is buying sales with credit terms rather than earning them; doing so while a large share of debt matures within the year converts reported revenue into an uncollected claim exactly when cash is required.
evaluated.reasoning: This abandons the capex rescaling for the one working-capital channel the archive has not tested — receivables measured *relative to the sales they finance*, which is the classic revenue-quality red flag and is distinct from the archived raw receivables growth leg that ignores whether sales grew alongside. The difference of two growth rates is naturally centred and scale-free, so it neither inherits the asset-growth main effect nor requires an unstable denominator.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cardinal Dual Overhang At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(ADD(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), SUB(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), MA(RATIO(SUB(SUB(act, che), invt), sale), 5))), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, lt)))
evaluated.hypothesis: Total operating liquidity consumed is the sum of the excess weeks of sales tied up in goods and the excess weeks tied up in customer credit, both measured against the firm's own normal operating level; that combined excess, amplified by the share of debt falling due within the year, is what leaves a firm unable to pay.
evaluated.reasoning: The two best specifications in the archive each captured one half of this — the dual channel gave the strongest slope (-4.09) in ordinal form, and the cardinal single channel gave the strongest Sharpe and coverage — and because both deviations are expressed in the same units (weeks of sales) they can be added directly rather than rank-averaged, which removes the weighting ambiguity that the critic raised against nested rank composites. This is the most complete statement of the mechanism this search has identified.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Structural Illiquidity Meets Rising Rollover Pressure
evaluated.hypothesis: A structurally illiquid balance sheet is survivable until creditors start shortening the firm's funding; the year in which the short-debt share jumps is the year the firm with no quick assets discovers it cannot roll, and that transition is what the market misprices.
evaluated.reasoning: Quick-asset scarcity has produced the largest alphas in this archive but never a cross-sectional slope, and the plausible reason is that it is a slow-moving structural characteristic already partly priced; pairing it with the *change* in maturity pressure converts it into an event-timing signal, which is the one specification that could supply the missing slope. It is also the only proposal in this batch whose investment leg is a balance-sheet stock rather than a working-capital flow, keeping the final generation from testing a single idea six times.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cardinal Overhang Against Uncovered Maturities
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(RATIO(dlc, ADD(dlc, che))))
evaluated.hypothesis: The relevant fragility is the fraction of near-term claims that cash cannot cover: a firm holding cash equal to its maturing debt faces no wall at all, while one holding almost none faces the whole of it, and that uncovered fraction is what turns excess inventory into a solvency problem.
evaluated.reasoning: Expressing coverage as dlc divided by dlc plus cash bounds the conditioner in the unit interval with a strictly non-negative denominator, which removes the near-zero and sign-flip pathologies the critic identified in the quick-asset denominator and guarantees the most constrained firms sit at the top of the rank rather than the bottom. It is also economically distinct from both archived conditioners: dlc/lt measures the composition of claims, while this measures the share of imminent claims with no cash behind them.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Cardinal Overhang Against Timing And Cover
evaluated.expression: MUL(WINSOR(SUB(RATIO(invt, sale), MA(RATIO(invt, sale), 5)), 1), RANK(SUMRANK(RATIO(dlc, lt), NEG(RATIO(ib, lt)))))
evaluated.hypothesis: Two independent things must be true for an inventory overhang to become a solvency event: the debt must fall due soon, and the firm's earnings must be too small to service the liability stock; timing without a cash-flow problem is refinanceable, and weak earnings without near-term maturities buys years of time.
evaluated.reasoning: The three-way stack was redundant with an archived conjunction, so instead this replaces the structural-illiquidity leg with debt-service capacity — a flow measure of fragility that has never been paired with the overhang mechanism, and which is economically orthogonal to the timing of claims. Combining the two conditioners inside a single bounded rank keeps the signed cardinal leg in control of the sort direction while adding a genuinely new economic condition rather than a second encoding of illiquidity.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Lean Stock With Improving Quick Position
evaluated.hypothesis: Resilience shows as a firm running its stock at the low end of its own history while its cash and receivables strengthen relative to what it owes in the next year; the operating discipline and the improving payment capacity together mark a firm that will not be forced into a distressed adjustment.
evaluated.reasoning: Rather than re-encoding the archived long-side signal, this changes both legs: the investment leg becomes a within-firm inventory *state* — the specification that beat flows repeatedly in this archive — and the conditioner becomes the improvement in the quick ratio, a payment-capacity trajectory never tested here and distinct from the maturity-mix change used before. Both legs are bounded ranks built from high-coverage annual items, so the long leg is populated by genuinely disciplined firms rather than by low-growth firms loading on CMA.
evaluated.author: proposer

evaluated.name: Peer-Relative Stock Excess At The Maturity Wall
evaluated.hypothesis: The benchmark that matters competitively is what rivals carry, not what the firm itself used to carry: a firm holding materially more weeks of stock than its industry is losing the demand race, and if its debt is also short-dated it must discount that stock to raise cash.
evaluated.reasoning: This replaces the hyperparameter tweak with a different economic benchmark — peers rather than own history — which captures competitive mispositioning rather than internal drift and answers a question the archive has never posed for the flagship mechanism. Because industry adjustment requires no time-series history, the coverage gain comes from removing a five-year lookback requirement rather than from admitting sparse-history firms, and the cardinal encoding preserves the magnitude weighting that produced the best Sharpe in generation 8.
evaluated.author: proposer

considered.name: Financing Gap Meets Illiquidity
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose capital spending exceeds operating cash flow must raise external funds; when it simultaneously holds little cash against near-term liabilities, the investment program is a genuine solvency risk rather than a growth option, and expected returns embed value destruction and dilution risk.
considered.reasoning: The capex-minus-operating-cash-flow gap measures external finance dependence directly, and the cash-to-current-liabilities term measures the buffer available to survive the funding period. Only the intersection — large gap plus thin liquidity — identifies fragile expansion, while a large gap at a cash-rich firm is ordinary growth investment. The interaction therefore isolates urgent balance-sheet strain rather than the isolated investment or liquidity effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory Buildup Under Working Capital Strain
considered.hypothesis: Rising inventories are benign when a firm has ample working capital but signal unsold product, forced production, and imminent liquidity trouble when net working capital is already negative, so the joint occurrence predicts subsequent write-downs and poor returns.
considered.reasoning: Inventory investment is the most reversible and most demand-sensitive component of firm investment, so it is the cleanest place to detect involuntary expansion. Conditioning on negative working capital separates a demand-driven stock build (financed comfortably) from a distress-driven one (financed by stretching payables). The interaction targets a mechanism distinct from fixed-capital or total-asset growth signals.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex Surge Against Cash-Flow Debt Service
considered.hypothesis: A firm spending far above its own recent capital-budget norm is only penalized when its operating cash flow is too thin to service existing liabilities; that combination signals an escalation that must be funded externally under stress, whereas a distressed firm spending below its own norm is credibly retrenching to preserve solvency.
considered.reasoning: The investment leg is a firm-relative capex surge (capex versus its own three-year average), not total asset growth, so it is orthogonal to the Cooper-Gulen-Schill construct and to CMA; the distress leg is the Beaver/Ohlson cash-flow-to-liabilities ratio rather than a leverage tilt. Centering the investment term with ZSCORE and weighting it by a distress rank in [0,1] makes the signal near-zero for financially sound firms, so the spread is a genuine interaction with an interpretable long leg (distressed retrenchers) rather than an amplified investment main effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Industry-Relative Capex Under Accumulated Deficit
considered.expression: MUL(IND_ZSCORE(RATIO(capx, at)), RANK(NEG(SUMRANK(RATIO(re, at), RATIO(wcap, at)))))
considered.hypothesis: Capital spending above industry norm is value-destroying specifically for firms carrying an accumulated earnings deficit and thin net working capital, because these firms lack the internal funds and liquidity slack to complete the program, while the same distressed firms spending below industry norm are conserving cash and are undervalued.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the binary retained-earnings dummy with a continuous, ranked two-component distress score (the retained-earnings and working-capital terms of the Altman construct) removes the mass of tied zeros, so both legs of the sort contain live firms and the signal varies within the distressed population as the hypothesis requires. Industry z-scoring the capex intensity strips out capital-intensity differences, ensuring the interaction reflects firm-specific aggressiveness rather than sector membership.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Levered Retrenchment Toward Liquidity
considered.expression: MUL(ZSCORE(WINSOR(SUB(DELTA(RATIO(che, at), 1), DELTA(RATIO(ppent, at), 1)), 1)), RANK(RATIO(lt, at)))
considered.hypothesis: Among highly levered firms, a deliberate rotation of the balance sheet out of fixed assets and into cash is a solvency-restoring action that the market underweights; the same rotation at an unlevered firm carries no information because there is no solvency constraint to relieve.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the additive asset-growth-plus-profitability composite (which FF5's CMA and RMW legs largely span) with a change-in-asset-composition variable that no standard factor prices: it is the shift in cash intensity minus the shift in fixed-capital intensity. Multiplying by the leverage rank makes the effect exist only where the mechanism operates, so the long leg is levered firms converting hard assets into liquidity and the short leg is levered firms sinking cash into fixed capital.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex Acceleration While Debt Ratio Rises
considered.hypothesis: Firms whose capital spending is accelerating at the same time their debt ratio is climbing are escalating commitment into a deteriorating capital structure and subsequently underperform, while firms decelerating capex as debt rises are prioritizing debt service and earn positive abnormal returns.
considered.reasoning: The prior version multiplied two signed changes, so escalation and orderly retrenchment produced identical positive values; replacing the leverage change with its cross-sectional rank in [0,1] makes the weight monotone and non-negative, so the signed capex-acceleration term alone determines direction and the two states are cleanly separated. Firms whose debt ratio is falling receive near-zero weight, which keeps the spread anchored on the deteriorating-solvency subpopulation the hypothesis describes while preserving full-cross-section coverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex Financed at Short Maturity
considered.hypothesis: Long-lived capital investment funded against a heavy stock of debt maturing within a year creates a maturity mismatch: the asset pays off over a decade while the liability must be rolled next quarter, so these firms bear rollover risk that is punished when credit conditions tighten.
considered.reasoning: This is a distinct fragility channel from leverage level or liquidity buffer — a firm can be modestly levered and still be dangerously short-funded — and it interacts naturally with the duration of the investment being made. The distress leg scales current debt by current assets, the pool actually available to retire it, so the signal isolates mismatch rather than size or leverage.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Headcount Expansion Without Debt Service Capacity
considered.hypothesis: Adding employees is a quasi-fixed commitment that is far harder to reverse than capex; when a firm expands headcount while earnings are too small relative to its liability stock, it is locking in an operating cost base it cannot fund, and subsequent layoffs and restructuring charges are underpriced.
considered.reasoning: This moves the investment leg off the balance sheet entirely and onto the real side, so it cannot be a rescaling of asset growth, capex intensity, or any accrual-based construct already in the archive. Because labor commitments carry no collateral value, the distress interaction should be sharper for employment growth than for capital growth — a directly testable contrast against the capex-based signals in this batch.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Levered Firms Sweating Installed Capacity
considered.hypothesis: Among highly levered firms, rising sales per unit of installed property and equipment shows management generating growth from assets already owned rather than from new commitments; this capital-efficient resilience is undervalued, while levered firms whose capacity utilization is falling are heading toward covenant trouble.
considered.reasoning: The gen-0 positive-sign attempt failed (alpha -1.7% against a positive prediction) because balance-sheet rotation into cash is itself a distress symptom rather than a discipline signal; utilization improvement is a genuine operating-performance channel that separates resilient levered firms from shrinking ones. Centering the utilization change and weighting by the leverage rank means unlevered firms contribute near zero, so both legs are populated by levered firms and the spread is an interaction rather than a leverage tilt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Stop-Start Capital Budgeting Under Deficit
considered.hypothesis: Erratic, stop-start capital spending reveals that a firm's investment is dictated by whatever financing happens to be available rather than by a stable opportunity set; when this instability coincides with an accumulated earnings deficit relative to the liability stock, projects get started and abandoned, sunk costs are written off, and returns disappoint.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the level-of-investment channel entirely for a second-moment channel — the volatility of the investment rate over three years — which is not a rescaling of capex intensity, asset growth, or any archived signal. The distress leg uses the accumulated deficit scaled by liabilities, a stock measure of never-having-earned that is conceptually independent of the flow coverage ratios used elsewhere in the archive, and the long leg is the economically meaningful case of fragile firms with steady, planned capital budgets.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Soft-Asset Expansion Without Earnings Cushion
considered.hypothesis: Expansion that adds intangible and goodwill-type assets rather than tangible capacity produces collateral that lenders will not accept and that must be impaired if performance disappoints; when the acquiring firm's pretax income is small relative to its liabilities, such soft-asset growth signals overpayment and imminent write-downs rather than franchise building.
considered.reasoning: The asset-quality composition of investment is a channel untouched by the archive, which has so far tested capex, inventory, headcount, and total-asset growth — all of which are collateralizable in a way intangibles are not, so the distress interaction should be sharply stronger here. Pretax income scaled by liabilities captures the debt-service cushion that determines whether an impairment triggers covenant trouble, giving a clean conditional reading rather than a repackaged profitability tilt.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Escalating Capex Into Deteriorating Profitability
considered.hypothesis: Distress is a trajectory, not a level: a firm whose return on assets has been sliding for several years and which nevertheless raises capital spending is escalating commitment to a failing business, while a firm on the same downward trajectory that cuts spending is adapting, and the market prices the two alike.
considered.reasoning: Replacing a static distress ratio with the multi-year slope of profitability makes the conditioning variable a state transition rather than an Altman-style level, so the signal cannot load on the RMW-like main effect that static profitability proxies carry. Centering the capex-growth leg while keeping the deterioration weight in [0,1] means healthy or improving firms contribute near zero, so both extremes of the sort are populated by deteriorating firms and the spread isolates the escalation-versus-adaptation contrast.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Fire-Sale Disinvestment Under Weak Coverage
considered.hypothesis: For firms whose earnings cannot cover their liability stock, shrinking the productive asset base is not disciplined retrenchment but forced liquidation at depressed prices, which destroys future earning capacity and predicts continued underperformance.
considered.reasoning: Every archived signal assumes the investment-distress relation is monotone decreasing, yet if distressed disinvestment is also punished the relation is U-shaped and the true mechanism is asset-base instability rather than overinvestment — a possibility no prior test can distinguish. This is the cheapest available test of that structural question, and it directly informs whether future long legs should be built from distressed retrenchers at all.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Inventory Growth Financed by Deteriorating Current Position
considered.hypothesis: Stock building is most dangerous when it is being financed by stretching payables and other current obligations, so that the current position is visibly deteriorating in the same year the inventory is added; the firm is converting near-term liquidity into unsold goods.
considered.reasoning: The archive's best-alpha inventory signal conditioned on the *level* of working capital, which the critic correctly noted is mechanically linked to inventory itself; conditioning instead on the *year-over-year deterioration in the current ratio* breaks that mechanical overlap and identifies the financing source of the buildup rather than its accounting footprint. This isolates static-versus-dynamic distress conditioning within the family that has worked best.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Sustained Investment While Deleveraging
considered.hypothesis: Investment carries opposite information depending on the direction of balance-sheet repair: a firm that maintains a high investment rate while simultaneously reducing its liability ratio is funding growth internally and demonstrating genuine operating strength, whereas the same investment rate alongside rising liabilities is externally financed expansion.
considered.reasoning: Both prior positive-sign attempts failed because they defined resilience as *low* investment, which loads on CMA and is indistinguishable from the published asset-growth effect; this defines resilience as high investment financed without new liabilities, which is the economically correct reading of self-funded capacity and is orthogonal to the conservative-investment factor. It is the direct mirror of the batch's negative signals and gives the long leg an interpretable, populated definition.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Building Into Shrinking Revenue
considered.hypothesis: Distress often arrives through the top line first: a firm whose revenue is contracting while it continues to add productive capacity is building assets for demand that has already disappeared, producing idle capacity, impairments, and eventual forced retrenchment.
considered.reasoning: This replaces the cash-slack conditioning the critic identified as double-counted with a demand-side fragility measure — revenue contraction — that appears nowhere in the archive and is conceptually independent of leverage, liquidity, and the cash balance. It also sharpens the mechanism: the destructive case is capacity added against falling demand, and the long leg is firms investing into genuine revenue growth, both of which are populated and interpretable.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Accumulated Capital Vintage Against Thin Equity Cushion
considered.hypothesis: What matters for a fragile firm is not this year's spending but the stock of recent commitments embedded in its asset base; a firm whose gross plant is mostly the product of the last five years' spending has an unproven, unamortized capital vintage, and if its book equity is thin relative to liabilities, any shortfall in the returns from that vintage is absorbed by creditors rather than cushioned.
considered.reasoning: This abandons the one-year escalation framing entirely for a stock-of-commitments channel — five-year cumulative capex as a share of gross plant measures how young and untested the installed base is, which no archived signal captures. The equity-to-liabilities cushion is a solvency variable (ceq is new to the archive) rather than a flow profitability measure, so the interaction cannot collapse into the q-theory investment-profitability effect.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Aging Capital Stock Under Current Liability Pressure
considered.hypothesis: A low ratio of net to gross plant means the asset base is heavily depreciated and has not been renewed; when the firm simultaneously faces current liabilities in excess of current assets, the deferred maintenance is a symptom of an inability to fund replacement capital, and competitive decline follows.
considered.reasoning: The tax framing is dropped because txt is effectively a profitability transform; this substitutes an asset-age channel measured purely from the plant accounts, which is a level concept absent from the archive and orthogonal to earnings. Paired with the accepted fire-sale disinvestment test, it lets the generation distinguish whether distressed *under*-investment is punished through forced sales, through deferred renewal, or not at all.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Acquisitions On A Thin Equity Base
considered.hypothesis: Acquisition spending is the least reversible and most agency-prone form of investment; undertaken by a firm whose book equity is thin relative to its asset base, it is effectively a levered bet where creditors bear the downside, and integration failure translates directly into solvency stress.
considered.reasoning: The acquisition channel is completely untested in the archive even though it is where the "value-destroying expansion" story is most literal, and treating an unreported aqc as zero acquisition activity is the economically correct convention rather than a coverage patch. Book-equity thinness is a solvency measure rather than a flow or liquidity measure, so the pairing does not replicate any existing distress leg.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Multi-Year Capacity Retreat Under Leverage
considered.hypothesis: A single year of shrinking plant is often ordinary depreciation or a disposal, but a productive asset base sitting at the bottom of its own five-year range signals a firm that has been retreating from its industry for years; when carried alongside heavy liabilities, that retreat is a solvency-driven withdrawal rather than a strategic focus.
considered.reasoning: The fire-sale test produced the archive's most reliable alpha but a wrong-signed slope because one-year plant growth is contaminated by the monotone asset-growth effect; replacing the change with a position-in-own-history state measures the persistence of retreat and should be far less collinear with that known force. If the slope and the alpha align here, it confirms that the disinvestment mechanism is real and that the earlier contradiction was a specification issue rather than an economic one.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capex Amid Lengthening Operating Cycle
considered.hypothesis: When non-cash current assets rise relative to sales, the firm is taking longer to convert production into cash — receivables are aging and goods are sitting — and a firm that adds fixed capacity while its operating cycle is stretching is committing long-term funds precisely as its short-term cash conversion deteriorates.
considered.reasoning: This drops the maturity-mismatch rescaling for a cash-conversion channel: the conditioner is the year-over-year change in working-capital intensity of revenue, which measures operating deterioration rather than the cash-holdings or short-debt dimensions already spanned by the archive. All four inputs are high-coverage balance-sheet and income items, so it should retain roughly 0.12 coverage while testing a fragility concept — operating-cycle stretch — that no archived signal contains.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Growth While Claims Outrun Revenue
considered.hypothesis: Solvency is a race between the growth of obligations and the growth of the revenue that must service them; a firm expanding gross plant while its liabilities compound faster than its sales is building capacity on a claim structure the business is not growing into.
considered.reasoning: Replacing the MIN experiment with a growth-rate mismatch makes the distress leg a dynamic solvency concept — the wedge between liability growth and revenue growth — rather than another level ratio drawn from the same balance-sheet dimensions already tested. It also avoids the correlation problem the critic identified, since the conditioner is a difference of growth rates and is close to orthogonal to the level of leverage, liquidity, or profitability.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Investing Through Chronic Losses
considered.hypothesis: One loss year is a shock; three or four losses in five years is a business model that does not work, and a firm that keeps its investment rate high across a sustained run of losses is funding a franchise the market has already learned cannot earn its cost of capital.
considered.reasoning: The extraordinary-items construct was accounting-incorrect, so the write-off idea is replaced by loss persistence — the count of loss years over five years, the Ohlson-style state variable — which the expression computes exactly and which no archived distress leg uses. Persistence is distinct from the *level* of profitability because a firm with a single deep loss year scores low here while a chronically marginal firm scores high, so the signal cannot collapse into the q-theory investment-profitability interaction.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Post-Investment Cash Surplus Among Levered Firms
considered.hypothesis: For a levered firm the decisive quantity is cash left after the capital program has been paid for, because that surplus is what retires debt; levered firms generating a post-investment surplus are deleveraging under their own power and are priced as if their leverage were a permanent risk, while levered firms with a post-investment deficit must return to markets.
considered.reasoning: The inverted ib/capx ratio is replaced by the correctly oriented free-cash-flow-after-investment measure, which is numerically stable, keeps capex in the numerator with the right sign, and is the exact quantity that determines debt-service capacity rather than a low-investment tilt. The leverage rank places unlevered firms near the middle of the sort, so both legs are populated by levered firms and the spread contrasts self-funding levered firms against externally dependent ones.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Forced Conservatism On A Thin Equity Cushion
considered.hypothesis: A firm whose gross plant is contracting and whose remaining plant is heavily depreciated is not practising capital discipline — it is unable to fund renewal; when its book equity is also thin relative to liabilities, the apparent conservatism is a solvency constraint, and the conservative-investment premium the market prices into such firms fails to materialise.
considered.reasoning: The three archived signals with the most reliable negative alphas each captured one facet of this state (plant contraction, asset age, multi-year retreat) separately; combining contraction and age into a single ranked disinvestment score should identify forced conservatism far more precisely than either leg alone while keeping both legs high-coverage. The equity cushion conditions on whether the retreat is voluntary, which is exactly the distinction the FF5 benchmark cannot make.
considered.author: proposer

considered.name: Capacity Contraction Against A Maturity Wall
